internal_claims.claim: Northbridge ran full diligence on an enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) developer, internally codenamed 'Thermalis,' which uses directional drilling techniques adapted from oil & gas to make geothermal viable outside traditional volcanic/tectonic-boundary regions; the firm reviewed their Series B raise within the past year.

Northbridge passed on Thermalis, but explicitly not due to technical skepticism about EGS as an approach - the firm's technical advisor assessed the underlying directional-drilling technology as reasonably de-risked given its oil & gas heritage, and the memo states this was a thesis-specific pass on one company, not a signal against enhanced geothermal broadly.

The pass on Thermalis was driven by two non-technical factors: (1) the company's model relied on continued cost deflation in directional drilling equipment that Northbridge viewed as optimistic given oilfield services pricing trends, and (2) offtake concentration risk, since their pipeline depended heavily on a single state's utility procurement program with uncertain multi-year funding.

During the Thermalis review, Northbridge informally tracked two other earlier-stage (seed/Series A) EGS developers without running full diligence, and observed both were pursuing a similar directional-drilling approach - suggesting this may be converging as the dominant technical approach in the EGS sub-segment rather than a differentiated bet unique to one company.

Northbridge's internal recommendation for any future EGS review is to weight offtake diversification and drilling-cost sensitivity more heavily in the investment model than technical feasibility, since technical feasibility was not the concern in the prior pass.

As of the most recent quarterly sector scan, inbound deal flow tagged 'enhanced geothermal' was roughly flat quarter-over-quarter, but the average stage of inbound has shifted later (fewer seed-stage intros, more Series B+), which the firm's sourcing team suggests may indicate the sub-segment is maturing past its earliest, most speculative phase.

Multiple LPs have asked Northbridge about its exposure to 'firm, dispatchable clean power' as a category spanning both advanced nuclear and enhanced geothermal, framed as a hedge against intermittent renewables' grid integration challenges; the firm notes this framing - dispatchability as a unifying thesis across sub-segments rather than separate bets - is a relatively new pattern in LP conversations worth incorporating into future sector briefings.

Northbridge's quarterly sector scan is explicitly caveated as directional and not verified, since it draws on inbound deal flow, LP conversations, and informal market chatter rather than confirmed data, meant to flag emerging patterns before any single sub-segment gets a formal diligence memo.

Northbridge's portfolio company Gridline Storage Systems (grid-scale battery storage) is not itself an EGS or geothermal company, but its CEO's comments on firm/dispatchable generation informed how Northbridge thinks about advanced nuclear and geothermal as complementary - rather than competing - bets; this is a portfolio check-in observation, not a geothermal-specific finding.

Gridline's CEO noted that utility customers are increasingly asking Gridline to model storage deployments alongside an assumed firm-generation source (advanced nuclear or geothermal specifically named in two recent customer conversations) rather than storage as a standalone solution to intermittency, reflecting a shift toward hybrid firm-plus-storage procurement models; Northbridge explicitly caveats this as one portfolio company's customer conversations, not a systematic survey.

external_claims.claim: Fervo Energy raised a $462 million Series E round in December 2025 to accelerate geothermal development and meet surging energy demand with clean, firm power.
Google, CalSTRS, and B Capital were among the backers of Fervo Energy's $462 million December 2025 funding round.
Fervo Energy secured $206 million in new financing in June 2025 to accelerate development, including $100 million in project-level preferred equity beginning in 2026.
Fervo Energy secured $255 million in new funding in December 2024, including a $120 million letter of credit facility, to deploy carbon-free geothermal power.
Fervo Energy completed its IPO on May 13, 2026 on the Nasdaq under ticker symbol 'FRVO', raising $1.89 billion at an implied valuation of $7.39 billion.
Fervo Energy's IPO price was set between $21.00 and $24.00 per share ahead of pricing.
Fervo Energy shares were expected to begin trading on Nasdaq on May 13, 2026 under ticker 'FRVO', with the offering closing shortly after.
Fervo Energy reported Q1 2026 capital expenditures of $172.8 million, compared to $105.4 million in Q1 2025, reflecting continued investment in its Cape Station project.
Fervo Energy's Cape Station Phase I is on track to begin delivering approximately 100 megawatts of power to the grid by late 2026, reaching full operating capacity by early 2027.
Fervo Energy's Cape Station project was upsized from 400 MW to 500 MW alongside a 31 MW power purchase agreement with Shell Energy announced in April 2025.
Eavor Technologies received an additional investment from Canada Growth Fund in June 2025 to support its Calgary-based advanced geothermal technology.
Eavor secured $421 million in non-recourse project financing for its Cape Station project in March 2026, described as establishing a commercial benchmark for the sector.

Sage Geosystems raised over $97 million in a Series B round co-led by Ormat Technologies and Carbon Direct Capital, announced January 21, 2026, to support development of its first commercial pressure geothermal power generation facility.
Sage Geosystems signed a deal with Meta in August 2024 to provide up to 150 megawatts, described as the first use of next-generation geothermal east of the Rocky Mountains.

Quaise Energy raised $134 million in the first close of its Series B round, announced July 7, 2026, to build what it describes as the world's first superhot geothermal power plant, bringing total funding raised to $230 million to date.
Quaise Energy raised a $21 million Series A1 round in March 2024, led by Prelude Ventures and Safar Partners, bringing its total funding at that time to more than $95 million.
XGS Energy completed an oversubscribed $13 million financing round (part of total funding of over $40 million to date at the time), reported in a filing dated around March-April 2025.
XGS Energy uses a proprietary 'solid-state geothermal system' with thermally conductive materials designed to deliver affordable energy at various locations.

A 2025 Stanford/Utah FORGE geothermal drilling cost curve update found vertical well drilling cost reductions of 12% to 24% and horizontal well cost reductions of 18% to 26%, based on results from Utah FORGE and Fervo Energy.
As of a 2026 industry report, drilling costs for a single deep enhanced geothermal well can exceed $14 million, concentrating significant financial risk before any project revenue is generated.

The IEA's flagship report (as covered in March 2026) featured superhot rock geothermal for the first time, stating the technology could compete with natural gas at $20-35 per megawatt-hour, and that up to $60 million will be provided to demonstrate enhanced geothermal drilling capability.
The U.S. DOE's Enhanced Geothermal Shot, launched September 8, 2022, targets a 90% cost reduction for EGS to $45 per megawatt-hour by 2035, equivalent to a target capital cost of $3,700/kW.
In January 2025, the Inflation Reduction Act's investment and production tax credits were expanded to cover geothermal power generation.
As of May 2025, geothermal policy analysts note that permitting timelines for a geothermal project in the U.S. can take between 5 and 10 years, underscoring the need for permitting reform.

A report covered in March 2026 found that enhanced geothermal deployment timelines could potentially be compressed to under three years, representing a 70% to 75% reduction from the historical seven-to-ten-year timeline.
Tech companies signed 14 geothermal power purchase agreements totaling 635 MW in 2025, a threefold increase from 2024, with data centers driving 60% of new geothermal capacity contracted.
Google signed a geothermal deal (reported February 2026) with Ormat Technologies to bring more geothermal resources onto the grid in Nevada to power data centers.

As of an August 2025 industry count, of 163 geothermal companies tracked, only 48 startups are funded and 31 have secured Series A financing, alongside more established companies such as Fervo Energy.

A geothermal heating project near a Danish town has faced repeated delays after drilling revealed underground rock conditions that were less predictable than expected, as reported in a recent (2026) update.
A commentary piece frames the current wave of enhanced geothermal investment as needing to be evaluated against historical patterns of hype versus practical technological and commercial limitations.

Utah FORGE successfully stimulated an injection well (16A(78)-32) and a production well (16B(78)-32), followed by a 9-hour circulation test that validated the approach, with drilling of the two first-of-their-kind wells occurring between October 2020 and April 2024.
